A device identity and its keys are generated on first launch and kept only on the device, encrypted at rest. Messages you send or receive are kept on your device and on the devices that carry them until they reach where they are going, or until you delete them. Nothing is uploaded to a server, because there is no server.
What nearby phones can and cannot see

A nearby phone can see that your device is present and can pass along messages addressed through it, the same way any phone in the mesh does. It cannot read a message that is not addressed to it: only the person you are writing to can read it.

Betar asks for Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct permissions to find and talk to nearby phones, and location permission only where the operating system requires it for that same nearby discovery, not to track where you are. It does not ask for internet access, contacts, or anything unrelated to passing messages between nearby devices.
Betar does not collect personal information from anyone, including children, because it does not collect personal information at all.
Every claim on this page is verifiable in the source code, and the app requests no internet permission at all, which anyone can confirm.
Use Betar to reach people nearby when the network cannot. Do not use it to harm, harass or deceive anyone you reach through it.
The software is provided as is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied.
Betar is maintained by its contributors as open source software, not by a company. No company is named here because none exists.

A message moves only when your phone comes within Bluetooth or Wi-Fi Direct range of another phone running Betar. There is no guarantee a message arrives, and no guarantee of how long it takes: minutes, hours, or never, depending entirely on which phones happen to be nearby and moving.
Betar cannot help if no other phone is in range. It carries messages between the phones that are actually present. It cannot conjure a path that does not exist.

The cryptography and protocol design follow established, published approaches, but the implementation has not yet had an independent audit. Treat it as you would any early-stage software handling sensitive communication: useful, actively developed, not yet independently verified.
Every permission Betar asks for exists to find and talk to nearby phones. Nothing else.
Bluetooth: to find and connect to nearby phones directly.
Wi-Fi Direct: a second, independent way to find and connect to nearby phones, used alongside Bluetooth.
Location: required by the operating system for nearby-device discovery on some Android versions, not used to track where you are.
Notifications: to show that mesh relay is running in the background.
Battery optimization exemption: so relay keeps working while the app is backgrounded. Optional.
Betar is AGPL-3.0: anyone may use, study, change and share it, and must keep a changed version open too.

Betar is a censorship-resistant social and chat app: no server to ban an account or remove a post, no SIM required, works over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct first. It is built on Project Mesh, the open protocol and Rust core that makes it work.
Betar (বেতার) is Bengali for wireless: literally be- (without) and tar (wire).

It honours Jagadish Chandra Bose. In November 1895, in Calcutta, he sent radio waves through two walls and a seated man\'s body to ring a bell and set off gunpowder in the next room, a public demonstration of wireless transmission before Marconi\'s own. He worked at millimetre wavelengths a century before ordinary phones got there, and he refused to patent any of it because he believed the work belonged to everyone.

He demonstrated wireless transmission publicly before Marconi and gave the work away unpatented. Whether he \"invented radio\" outright is genuinely contested, and this project makes no claim beyond what the historical record supports.
Betar is open source under AGPL-3.0. Same idea, roughly a hundred and thirty years later.

Project Mesh is the name of the open protocol and the Rust core underneath: identity, encryption, message routing, the pieces that make phone to phone delivery work without a server. Betar is the application built on top of it, and the name most people will actually use.
